title: Memento
objectives: Capture a valid state without exposing its private fields.
Distinguish local restoration from reversing external effects.
Design history consumption and capacity rules.

sections.heading: The problem: remember an interval without breaking its rules
paragraphs: A chart lets a reader select an inclusive interval from zero through one hundred. The low endpoint must never exceed the high endpoint. A change sets both endpoints together, and undo should restore the previous pair. One direct approach keeps two old integer variables beside the user-interface code. That is enough for a single local operation when the state is already public. The problem appears when the selection owns private state and more callers need undo without learning how that state is stored.

Exposing low_ and high_ so a history manager can copy them creates two risks. A caller can change only one endpoint and leave an invalid interval. Also, adding another part of selection state forces every outside snapshot routine to change. The object that understands the rules should produce its own saved record. The history manager should store that record without reading or editing its contents. A saved record with this role is a memento, also called a snapshot.

sections.heading: Let the state owner define the snapshot boundary
paragraphs: Selection keeps low_ and high_ private. Its set operation accepts both values, validates all conditions, and changes neither member if the pair is invalid. The Snapshot nested class also keeps its two integers private. Its constructor is private, so outside code cannot construct an arbitrary invalid pair disguised as a valid snapshot. friend class Selection grants Selection access to those private members and constructor. Friendship is a specific access permission; it is not inheritance, ownership, or a promise that all surrounding classes can inspect the record.

Snapshot publicly supports copying. This lets a History store snapshots in a vector without seeing their fields. Selection::save builds a snapshot from the current valid pair and returns it by value. Modern C++ can construct that returned value directly in its destination; whether a small copy is removed does not change the ownership contract. The snapshot owns two independent integers, so later edits to Selection cannot change what the snapshot remembers. A snapshot that stored references to live endpoints would fail this basic requirement.

sections.heading: Restoration should have a clear failure story
paragraphs: restore takes a const Snapshot& and copies both integers back. It borrows the saved record for the duration of the call and leaves that record unchanged. Because these integer assignments cannot allocate or throw, restoration cannot stop between endpoints through a C++ exception in this implementation. This is an exception-safety guarantee for local operations, not a statement that another thread cannot see an intermediate assignment. The program is single-threaded and requires external synchronization if shared.

The snapshot stores the entire selected interval and nothing else. It does not store the chart pixels, a mouse position, a disk file, or the number of saved history entries. Those choices form the snapshot boundary: which state is restored together. Including too little produces inconsistent restoration; including unrelated state makes undo surprisingly broad. Here any Snapshot created by any Selection can be restored into another Selection because every instance uses the same range rules. The test demonstrates that portable value policy. A per-document or per-session policy would need an identity token and an explicit rejection rule.

sections.heading: The history manager keeps records without opening them
paragraphs: History borrows a Selection and owns a vector of Snapshot values. remember asks the selection for a snapshot and stores it. undo returns false for an empty vector, making the lack of history an ordinary result rather than an exceptional failure. Otherwise it restores the last snapshot and only then removes that snapshot. The order expresses a useful general rule: do not consume the recovery record before the restoration it supports has succeeded.

In this example restoration cannot throw, but retaining the order makes later changes easier to reason about. If snapshots later include a string or collection, restoring field by field could allocate and fail halfway through. A stronger design could build a complete proposed state first and swap it into place with a nonthrowing operation. The caretaker, the common pattern name for a history manager, should not guess how to do that. The object that owns the state must preserve its own invariants during restoration.

sections.heading: A snapshot is a value, not a rewind button for the world
paragraphs: The sample saves [2,5], changes the selection to [20,40], and restores [2,5]. It also keeps a separate snapshot variable and restores it more than once. This is valid because restore does not consume the snapshot. History choosing to pop its last record is a policy of that history, not a property of all snapshots. A history can instead support named checkpoints, multiple branches, or repeated restore to one baseline. Each needs a clear rule for which records remain available.

Restoring an interval does not undo an exported image that was already sent to another person. A snapshot covers local state inside its declared boundary. It also does not automatically provide persistence across program runs: the program stores C++ values in memory and defines no file format. Persistent snapshots need versioned data, validated loading, and a plan for fields that change between software versions. Calling a memory snapshot a backup would mislead users unless those additional guarantees exist.

sections.heading: Bound memory growth without weakening the contract
paragraphs: Unlimited history stores more records after every remember call. For two integers this seems cheap, but a rich document may hold large images or trees. A capacity limit is therefore a product choice as well as a memory choice: the user can undo only so far. The lab retains the newest three remembered states. It builds a proposed vector, removes the oldest item if necessary, appends the new snapshot, then swaps the proposed vector into place. If allocation fails before the swap, the original history remains available.

A complete copied snapshot is easiest to reason about but may be costly. An alternative stores only the changed values, called a delta, or uses command-specific undo as in Chapter 14. Another approach shares immutable data between snapshots. These designs can save memory but add dependencies between records or more demanding ownership rules. Measure the actual state size and editing pattern. Do not replace a few cheap copied values with a complicated history graph merely because the latter sounds more advanced.

example.title: An opaque snapshot of a valid chart interval
requirements: Capture and restore both endpoints as one logical state.
Let History store records without reading their private values.
example.design: Selection creates a private nested Snapshot containing copied integers. History owns snapshots by value and borrows the selection. Restoration leaves the snapshot reusable and history consumes a record only after restore.
example.alternative: For one local edit, saving two old integers is enough. Command-specific inverse operations can reduce storage for large changes, but require correct reverse behavior. Shared immutable snapshots help large documents at the cost of more ownership design.
invariants: Every Selection pair is valid before and after public operations.
A saved snapshot is unaffected by later changes to its source.
History must not outlive the Selection it borrows.
Cross-instance restore is allowed because instances share the same value rules.

failures.mistake: Snapshot stores references to low_ and high_ instead of copied values.
failures.consequence: After setting [20,40], the alleged old snapshot also reads [20,40].
failures.reason: It observes current storage rather than retaining the old state.

failures.mistake: Assign low_ before validating high and low together.
failures.consequence: A rejected set(9,3) may leave the interval partially changed and invalid.
failures.reason: Throwing does not undo earlier assignments automatically.

example.verification: The program checks empty history, restore of both endpoints, snapshot reuse, invalid-pair rejection without mutation, boundary [0,100], and cross-instance restoration. It does not test persistence, concurrency, or allocation failures in history growth.
example.maintenance: The state owner retains control of representation and valid restoration. Whenever a new field is added, review whether it belongs inside the snapshot boundary and add a restore test for that choice.

diagram.title: History holds records; Selection defines their meaning
diagram.explanation: The History-to-Snapshot edge means owned value storage. History-to-Selection is a borrowed dependency. Selection can read Snapshot internals because of friendship, a C++ access rule; the creation/read arrow is a teaching dependency and does not mean Selection owns every saved snapshot.

focus.title: Copy the interval into and out of a record
focus.what: These operations define exactly which state a snapshot captures.
focus.where: Selection owns both operations because it knows its private representation.
focus.why: Outside history code can keep a value without accessing either endpoint.
focus.invariant: Both endpoints are copied, and saved values remain unchanged.
focus.risk: Reference-based snapshots would track live changes instead of preserving history.

The comment says the pair is copied together.

focus.title: Restore first, consume history second
focus.what: This operation restores the newest saved state if one exists.
focus.where: History supplies ordering but cannot inspect snapshot fields.
focus.why: The recovery record should remain available until restoration succeeds.
focus.invariant: An empty history returns false and changes no selection state.
focus.risk: Popping before a potentially throwing restore would lose the only record needed to retry.

The comment states the normal empty-history case.

trace.reason: save makes independent copies of both integers.
Changing the live object does not alter the saved value.
The last record restores both fields before being removed.
The whole pair is validated before either assignment.

trace.state: Another Selection restores the saved record to [2,5].
trace.reason: This design intentionally treats snapshots as portable interval values.

summary: A snapshot should own the state it promises to remember.
The originator controls access and restoration rules.
A history manager can store opaque records.
State boundaries determine what undo actually restores.
Local memory snapshots do not imply persistent backups or reversal of external effects.

exercises.prompt: Change the allowed maximum from one hundred to two hundred. Which existing boundary test changes, and what new rejected case should be added?
exercises.hint: The validation rule is centralized in Selection::set.
exercises.answer: Allow high <= 200, test [0,200], and reject [0,201] without changing the existing selection. Snapshot fields and history need no structural change because the representation is still two integers.

exercises.prompt: Starting at [1,4], remember; set [3,8], remember; set [6,9]; undo twice. List the state after each undo.
exercises.hint: History stores state when remember is called.
exercises.answer: The first undo restores [3,8] and the second restores [1,4]. Saving after a change records a different checkpoint than saving before it; the caller must choose that policy deliberately.

exercises.prompt: An undo implementation pops the last record and then tries to restore it through a reference previously obtained from back(). What is wrong?
exercises.hint: The referenced vector element has been destroyed.
exercises.answer: The reference dangles after pop_back. Accessing it is undefined behavior, even if the memory still contains old bits. Restore before popping, or first copy the snapshot into an independent local value.

exercises.prompt: A snapshot of an image editor would copy hundreds of megabytes after each keystroke. Name two alternatives and explain one tradeoff.
exercises.hint: Retain only changes or share data that cannot change.
exercises.answer: Command-specific deltas store smaller changes but require correct inverse operations. Shared immutable image blocks let snapshots reuse unchanged data, but need clear ownership and a new block whenever content changes.

exercises.prompt: Limit history to its newest three records. For remembered low values one, two, three, four with high=low+1, which undo values remain?
exercises.hint: Remove the oldest checkpoint, not the newest.
exercises.answer: Undo returns low values four, three, two, then false. One has been discarded. The reference solution builds proposed history before committing so allocation failure does not erase an old record first.

exercises.prompt: Explain whether restoring one Selection snapshot into another should be allowed. Give both a valid policy and when you would reject it.
exercises.hint: Consider whether state values have owner-specific meaning.
exercises.answer: It is allowed here because all selections use the same coordinate range. Reject it for document-specific coordinates or ownership-sensitive resources unless the snapshot carries and validates a matching identity. Either policy can be sound when explicit and tested.

lab.task: Change History::remember so only the three most recent snapshots remain. Preserve the old history if creating the proposed new history throws before commit. Keep all primary behavior and add a four-record eviction test.
checks: An empty history and invalid Selection update still behave as before.
lab.answer: The solution copies saved_ into proposed, evicts the oldest item there, appends a new snapshot, and swaps. The original vector is untouched until commit. A fixed-capacity buffer would avoid allocation during ordinary updates, but requires its own careful ordering and overwrite tests.

glossary.definition: A saved record of object state whose details are controlled by the state owner.
The object that creates and interprets its own snapshots.
An object that keeps snapshots without managing their internal representation.
The set of state restored together by one snapshot.

problem_title: Restore a valid state without exposing its parts

attachment_alignment.epub_section: Memento: restoring editor state, originator/memento/caretaker roles, nested snapshot design, and combining snapshots with Command.
attachment_alignment.intent: Preserve an object’s prior state so it can be restored without making outside history code understand its private representation. The EPUB starts with editor undo and the danger of having another object copy private fields. The object that owns the state must decide what a valid snapshot contains and how restoration works.
attachment_alignment.mechanism: The originator creates a memento containing saved state. A caretaker keeps those records and chooses when to restore one. The originator interprets the record and restores its own invariants. The caretaker manages history policy rather than field-level copying. Capturing independent values is essential: references to live fields would remember future changes rather than past state.

roles.responsibility: Own current state and define save/restore operations. Selection validates both endpoints together and decides the snapshot boundary.
Retain an independent state record. The new nested value has private endpoints and a private constructor.
Keep records in order and decide when to restore one. History cannot inspect or edit snapshot endpoints.
Choose when to remember relative to edits. A snapshot taken before a change records a different checkpoint from one taken afterward.

source_walkthrough: ClientCode creates Originator with an initial string, then repeats Backup followed by DoSomething three times. Backup asks Save for a newly allocated ConcreteMemento. DoSomething replaces the live string with thirty generated characters. The saved records therefore hold the initial state, first changed state, and second changed state.

ShowHistory prints each record’s name and date. The first Undo removes the newest pointer from history and asks Originator::Restore to recover the second changed state. The next Undo restores the first changed state. Restore deletes the supplied memento after copying its string; the caretaker destructor later deletes records still held in its vector.

The attached output includes dated, generated strings. Those literal values are one recorded run, not portable expected output: main seeds the generator from the current time. Also, the supplied Memento interface publicly exposes state(), despite its comments describing restricted state access. The caretaker chooses not to call it, but C++ does not prevent that access.
attachment_alignment.adaptation: The new example follows the EPUB’s opaque-snapshot intent more strictly: only Selection is a friend allowed to inspect Snapshot fields. C++ requires this explicit access grant; nesting alone does not give the outer class access to nested private members. Random text and dates become deterministic interval values. Snapshot values replace owning raw pointers, and restore borrows rather than consumes a record. History restores before popping. The example omits history labels and persistent storage while adding invalid-state, reuse, and cross-instance tests.
attachment_alignment.recognize: Identify who creates the record, who understands its contents, and who only keeps it. Here Selection does the first two jobs and History does the third. A plain copy is not enough to explain the design: the snapshot boundary and controlled restoration are what protect the state owner when its representation changes.

contrast.distinction: Command records a requested action. Memento records state. A command may keep a memento before acting, then use it for undo; neither pattern requires the other.
Prototype creates another usable object by copying an existing one. A memento is a restricted recovery record for selected state, not necessarily a full working duplicate.

teach.action: Label initial state S0 and changed states S1, S2, S3. Record the three backups, then predict S2 and S1 after the two undo calls.
Compare the supplied public state() operation with the new Snapshot private fields. Explain which restriction the compiler now enforces.
Save [2,5], change to [20,40], and undo. Attempt [9,3], then reuse the separate snapshot. Ask which operations consume history and which merely borrow a record.

checks.question: Does the supplied first Undo restore the initial state?
checks.answer: No. Three backups were made before three changes. The newest backup holds S2, so the first undo restores S2 and the second restores S1.

checks.question: Why may History copy Snapshot but not edit its endpoints?
checks.answer: Copying preserves an entire valid saved value through public copy operations. Private fields and the private constructor prevent the caretaker from manufacturing a different endpoint pair.
